title: Far apart: knowledge and ignorance
theme: Ignorance and knowledge lie far apart and lead opposite ways; Death judges Naciketas a seeker of knowledge, since no desire tore him away.

words.role: first member of the pair, in a relative clause
subject of [the understood] ज्ञाता with अविद्या and of ज्ञाता with विद्या
main verb of the second sentence (Death speaks)
main verb of the last clause

sandhi.rule: The m stays before a vowel.
viṣūcī is a dual ending in ī and so pragṛhya, P. 1.1.11 (ईदूदेद्द्विवचनं प्रगृह्यम्); it does not combine with the following a, P. 6.1.125 (प्लुतप्रगृह्या अचि नित्यम्).

sandhi.type: āḥ before a voiced consonant; aḥ before a
sandhi.rule: kāmāḥ before b: the visarga becomes y, P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि), which is dropped before a consonant, P. 8.3.22 (हलि सर्वेषाम्). bahavaḥ before a: P. 6.1.113 (अतो रोरप्लुतादप्लुते), P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः), P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति).

sandhi_exceptions.note: viṣūcī avidyā: the dual viṣūcī is pragṛhya, P. 1.1.11 (ईदूदेद्द्विवचनं प्रगृह्यम्), and does not combine with the following vowel, P. 6.1.125 (प्लुतप्रगृह्या अचि नित्यम्).

samasa.meaning: one who longs for knowledge; Śaṅkara and Raṅgarāmānuja: «विद्यार्थिनं»

morphology.note: Feminine dual of viṣvañc ‘turned in different directions’, in the Vedic form in -ī; the classical form is viṣūcyau, which Śaṅkara gives as his gloss: «विषूची विषूच्यौ».

Raṅgarāmānuja analyses it as the imperfect of the intensive of lup, citing P. 3.1.24 (लुपसदचरजपजभदहदशगॄभ्यो भावगर्हायाम्), with a Vedic loss of y (lolupya- > lolup-): «छान्दसो यलोपः»; or as the intensive without its suffix, with a Vedic middle ending and no augment: «यङ्लुगन्ताद्वा छान्दसमात्मनेपदम्, अडभावश्च». In the text the augment a- is hidden by the sandhi bahavo ’lolupanta.
abhīpsin ‘longing for’: abhi + īps, the desiderative of āp ‘obtain’, with the agent suffix -in.

translation.literal: ‘Far apart [are] these two, opposed, going different ways: what is known as ignorance and [what is known] as knowledge. I consider Naciketas one who longs for knowledge; desires, many [as they were], did not tear you away.’
translation.readable: ‘Ignorance and what is called knowledge are far apart; they are opposites and lead in opposite directions. I see that Naciketas longs for knowledge: all those desires could not pull you away.’

anvaya: या अविद्या, या च विद्या इति ज्ञाता, एते दूरम् विपरीते विषूची [च] । नचिकेतसम् विद्याभीप्सिनम् मन्ये । बहवः कामाः त्वा न अलोलुपन्त ।
syntax: Three clauses. A nominal sentence with the dual subject ete and two dual predicates (viparīte, viṣūcī), explained by the relative clause avidyā yā ca vidyeti jñātā, where yā serves both nouns. Then Death’s judgement, with a double accusative (naciketasaṃ vidyābhīpsinaṃ manye), and its reason, the many desires did not tear you away; Death passes from the third person (Naciketas) to the second (tvā).

ambiguities.note: The base and the other witnesses read vidyābhīpsinam, ‘longing for knowledge’. Madhva’s text reads vidyābhīpsitam (corrections.json). Raṅgarāmānuja knows that reading and explains it as a compound with the participle placed last, as in āhitāgni: «‘विद्याभीप्सितम्’ इति पाठे आहिताग्नयादित्वात् निष्ठान्तस्य परनिपातः», so that it means the same.
Madhva’s text reads bahavo lolupantaḥ, a participle, ‘[you, whom] many greedy desires [did not move]’ (corrections.json). The base reading is a finite verb with a hidden augment.

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: The halves count 21 and 23: the pādas have 11, 10, 12 and 11 syllables. avidyā yā ca vidyeti jñātā has 10; vidyābhīpsinaṃ naciketasaṃ manye has 12. The hiatus viṣūcī avidyā is counted as written.

beginner: Death now says something about two ways of living, which he calls ignorance and knowledge. They are not just a little different; they lie far apart and lead in opposite directions, like light and darkness, as one commentator puts it. Ignorance here is the life that follows the pleasant; knowledge is the life that follows the good. Then Death turns to the boy and gives his judgement: Naciketas wants knowledge. Death knows this because he tested him. He offered many desirable things, and none of them could pull the boy away from what he had asked. A person’s real wish is shown by what he refuses, not only by what he says he wants. The test is over, and the teaching can begin.
analogy: Like two roads that leave the same crossroads in opposite directions: a few steps apart at first, they end very far from each other.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That ignorance and what is called knowledge are far apart, opposed and divergent; and that he judges Naciketas to be one who longs for knowledge, because many desires could not tear him away.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: because one is discrimination and the other its absence, like darkness and light, «विवेकाविवेकात्मकत्वात् तमःप्रकाशाविव»; they lead to different results, worldly existence and release, «विषूच्यौ नानागती भिन्नफले संसारमोक्षहेतुत्वेनेत्येतत्». Ignorance concerns the pleasant, knowledge the good: «या च अविद्या प्रेयोविषया विद्येति च श्रेयोविषया».

commentary.q: What are knowledge and ignorance for Raṅgarāmānuja?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Ignorance is made of desire and action, «कामकर्मात्मिका»; knowledge consists of dispassion and knowledge of the truth, «वैराग्यतत्त्वज्ञानमयी». The desires did not break him from the path of the good: «श्रेयोमार्गाद्विच्छेदं न कृतवन्तः».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: An intensive of lup ‘break, tear away’. Raṅgarāmānuja cites P. 3.1.24 (लुपसदचरजपजभदहदशगॄभ्यो भावगर्हायाम्) for the intensive and notes the Vedic irregularities: «छान्दसो यलोपः», or a Vedic middle and no augment, «अडभावश्च». Śaṅkara glosses the sense: the desires did not cut him off, «न विच्छेदं कृतवन्तः».

advaita.text: Knowledge and ignorance are as opposed as light and darkness and cause release and worldly existence respectively; Naciketas, unmoved by desire, is a fit vessel of the good: «अतो विद्यार्थिनं श्रेयोभाजनं मन्ये इत्यभिप्रायः».

visistadvaita.text: Ignorance is desire and action, knowledge is dispassion and knowledge of the truth; the boy is not under the sway of objects: «विषयवशगो न भवसि इत्यर्थः».

schools.disagreement: Śaṅkara and Raṅgarāmānuja agree on the verse. Śaṅkara defines the pair by discrimination (viveka), Raṅgarāmānuja by its content (desire and action against dispassion and knowledge of the truth). Madhva comments on the passage 1.2.4–8 only at 1.2.8; his text has two variants here.

contemporary.text: Teachers often learn more about a student’s seriousness from what the student turns down than from what the student says. Death’s judgement of Naciketas rests on exactly that: the offers refused. The verse also insists that the two directions are not a little apart but far apart — a reminder that small daily preferences add up to very different lives. This is a reflection, not part of the commentaries.

reflect.beginner: What have you turned down recently, and what did that show about what you want?
reflect.deeper: Why would the Upaniṣad call the life of the pleasant ‘ignorance’ rather than ‘wrongdoing’?
reflect.practice: Notice one small preference today and ask which of the two directions it leans.

flags.note: Madhva’s text reads vidyābhīpsitam and lolupantaḥ (corrections.json); Raṅgarāmānuja knows and explains the first.
